summary.text: The Iceland hotspot is a hotspot that is partly responsible for the heavy volcanism that built the island of Iceland and the Iceland Plateau.
Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where two plates pull apart, but the hotspot helps explain why it is a large island while most of the ridge stays below sea level.
Scientists still debate whether it is fed by a deep mantle plume or comes from a much shallower source.

facts.label: Eruption rate
facts.value: Roughly one eruption every three years on average

facts.label: Share of lava
facts.value: About a third of basalt erupted in recorded history

facts.label: Biggest witnessed eruption
facts.value: Eldgjá in 934, the largest basaltic one seen

facts.label: Oldest crust
facts.value: Over 20 million years old, in the Westfjords

items.prompt: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is mostly a line of underwater peaks, yet at Iceland it rises into a large island. What best explains the difference?

options.label: The plates pull apart faster there than anywhere else
A hotspot adds extra volcanism on top of the spreading
Sea level is much lower in the North Atlantic
Glaciers piled rock up into a high plateau

items.explain: Plate separation alone does not explain it; an extra cause, the hotspot, is needed to make Iceland a substantial island.

items.prompt: Besides being hotter, the mantle under Iceland is thought to hold more water. How could that boost the volcanism?

options.label: Water cools the mantle so it rises faster
Water turns to steam that lifts the island
Water makes rock melt at a lower temperature
Water dissolves the crust above the mantle

items.explain: Water in magma lowers the melting temperature, which may help enhance Icelandic volcanism.

items.prompt: When an Icelandic volcano erupts beneath an ice cap, what danger often follows?

options.label: A sudden flood of glacial meltwater
The ice cap freezes the lava solid
A deep sinkhole swallows the glacier
The eruption is fully smothered by ice

items.explain: Several eruptions beneath ice caps have produced devastating glacial bursts, most recently after Eyjafjallajökull in 2010.

items.prompt: Geologists find an extinct spreading ridge in western Iceland, while today's active volcanic zones lie farther east. What does that suggest?

options.label: The island has been rotating in place
Western Iceland is sinking into the sea
The plates have stopped moving apart
The main activity has shifted east over time

items.explain: The extinct western ridge led to the idea that the plume has shifted east, and the spreading centre has jumped eastward more than once.

items.prompt: The oldest volcanic rocks linked to the Iceland plume, 64 to 58 million years old, lie on both sides of the Atlantic. What has this led some to suggest?

options.label: Its arrival may have helped split the continents
Lava flowed across an ocean that already existed
Two separate plumes formed at the same time
The rocks were carried over later by glaciers

items.explain: Those ages match the opening of the north Atlantic, suggesting the plume's arrival was linked to, and perhaps contributed to, the breakup of Laurasia.

items.prompt: Some geologists argue there is no deep plume under Iceland at all. What do they say drives its volcanism instead?

options.label: Heat from the Earth's core leaking up directly
Repeated impacts by large meteorites
Plate tectonic processes within the upper mantle
Friction from glaciers grinding on the rock

items.explain: Weak plume images in the lower mantle and chemical evidence led to the view that the volcanism comes from plate-related processes in the upper mantle.
